summary.text: An atoll is a ring-shaped island made of a coral rim around a lagoon, sometimes with small coral islands or cays on the rim.
In Darwin's subsidence model, a fringing reef around a volcanic island becomes a barrier reef and then an atoll as the island sinks completely beneath the sea.
Because reef-building corals thrive only in warm water, the world's roughly 440 atolls lie in the tropics and subtropics, most of them in the Pacific.

facts.label: Origin of the word
facts.value: Dhivehi atholhu, a language of the Maldives

items.prompt: According to Darwin's model, what fills the middle of an atoll?

options.label: The flooded crater of the old volcano
A freshwater lake fed by rain
A lagoon where the sunken volcano used to be
A pile of sand washed in by storms

items.explain: A lagoon takes the place of the former volcano after it sinks, but the lagoon is not the old volcanic crater.

items.prompt: You want to visit atolls. Where should you look?

options.label: Only in tropical and subtropical seas
In polar seas, where ice shelters the reefs
Along any coast that has volcanoes
Mostly in cold, deep northern waters

items.explain: Reef-building corals thrive only in warm tropical and subtropical waters, so atolls are found only there.

items.prompt: For a long time, the sea rises faster than an atoll's coral can grow. What happens to the atoll?

options.label: The island floats up with the rising water
The reef drops below the surface and the atoll is lost
The lagoon dries up and becomes a forest
The reef spreads outward and the atoll grows

items.explain: An atoll persists only if coral growth keeps the reef at the sea surface, matching any change in sea level.

items.prompt: In the antecedent karst model, a flat coral island sits exposed to rain for ages. Why does it end up shaped like a saucer?

options.label: Waves wear down the rim faster than the middle
Coral grows fastest at the island's centre
A volcano under the centre collapses inward
Rain dissolves the centre faster than the rim

items.explain: Rain dissolves the exposed coral into karst, slowest along the rim and fastest at the centre, leaving a raised rim around a hollow.

items.prompt: Bermuda, at 32° N, is too far north for coral reefs to form on their own. Why does it have them anyway?

options.label: Heat from an undersea volcano warms its reefs
Its corals are cold-water species from the deep
The warm Gulf Stream heats the water around it
Long summer days give its corals extra sunlight

items.explain: At Bermuda's latitude, coral reefs would not develop without the warming waters of the Gulf Stream.

items.prompt: Seen from above, how much of a typical atoll is dry land?

options.label: A small share; reef and lagoon make up most
Most of it, with only a little lagoon
About half land and half water
All of it, since the lagoon is fenced off

items.explain: In most cases an atoll's land area is very small compared with its total area.

paragraphs.heading: A ring of coral
paragraphs.text: An atoll is an island shaped like a ring: a rim of coral that surrounds a lagoon. Small coral islands, or cays, may sit on the rim. In most atolls the dry land is only a small part of the total area. The islands are low, rising less than 5 metres above the sea.

paragraphs.heading: Where atolls are found
paragraphs.text: Reef-building corals thrive only in warm tropical and subtropical seas, so that is the only place atolls occur. Of roughly 440 atolls in the world, most lie in the Pacific, in groups such as the Marshall Islands, Kiribati and Tuvalu, or in the Indian Ocean, including the Maldives. The Atlantic has no large groups of them, apart from eight atolls east of Nicaragua in the Caribbean.

paragraphs.heading: Darwin's sinking island
paragraphs.text: In 1842 Charles Darwin explained atolls using what he had seen on the voyage of HMS Beagle. A coral fringing reef forms around a volcanic island. Over geologic time the volcano dies, wears away and sinks below the waves, while the reef turns into a barrier reef cut off from the island. In the end only the reef and its small islets remain, with a lagoon where the volcano once stood, though the lagoon is not the old crater. For the atoll to last, the coral must grow fast enough to match the sinking island or the rising sea.

paragraphs.heading: A second explanation
paragraphs.text: Another idea is called the antecedent karst model. First, a flat-topped coral mound forms as an island sinks below sea level. When the sea later falls, the mound is left in the open air, and rain dissolves it into limestone karst. The middle dissolves fastest and the rim slowest, leaving a saucer with a raised edge. When the sea rises again, coral regrows on the rim to make the islands, and the flooded centre becomes the lagoon.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word comes from
paragraphs.text: The word atoll comes from atholhu in Dhivehi, an Indo-Aryan language of the Maldives. It reached French as atollon in 1625. Darwin later used it to mean a circular group of coral islets.

paragraphs.heading: Record holders
paragraphs.text: The northernmost atoll is Kure Atoll at 28°25′ N, in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. The southernmost are Elizabeth Reef and Middleton Reef in the Tasman Sea. Aranuka in Kiribati sits closest to the Equator, its southern tip only 13 km north of it. Huvadhu Atoll in the Maldives has the most islands, 255 in all.
